Chapter 8
VLANs and Inter-VLAN Routing

This manual replaces Chapter 8 of Todd Lammle, CCNA Certification Study Guide, Volume 2, Exam 200-301 (2020), book pages 219 to 250. It follows the book's order and numbering, keeps the book's learning objectives, and marks every place where this document differs from the book, so you always know what is from the book and what is not.

Read it top to bottom: pre-check, sections 8.1 to 8.4, troubleshooting, labs, review questions, then the revision sheet and tracker table. Nothing here was run on real Cisco equipment. Where a command or output was not run, it is marked CHECK .

WHAT THE BOOK SAYS
Learning objectives (from the book, p. 219)
2.0 Network Access (v1.0 numbering used by the book)
2.1 Configure and verify VLANs (normal range) spanning multiple switches: 2.1.a Access ports (data and voice); 2.1.b Default VLAN; 2.1.c Connectivity.
2.2 Configure and verify interswitch connectivity: 2.2.a Trunk ports; 2.2.b 802.1Q; 2.2.c Native VLAN.
The chapter also teaches how VLANs break up broadcast domains, how frame tagging works, and how to route between VLANs with a router on a stick and with a Layer 3 switch (SVIs).
VERIFY

Verification note. Every subnet, mask, broadcast and host range in this chapter (the book's Figures 8.12 to 8.15, my lab addressing, and the review questions) was calculated with a Python ipaddress script. All four of the book's worked examples came out correct. The script and its output were run in this session.
What was not done: no command in this document was run on a Cisco switch, router or simulator. Packet Tracer and real IOS behaviour can differ from what is written here.

Book pages 220 to 224. Tracker rows: 8.1, 8.1.1, 8.1.2, 8.1.3. v1.1 objective 2.1. v2.0 objective 2.2.

The idea in plain words. A switch sends a broadcast out of every port except the one it arrived on. So one switch with no VLANs is one big broadcast domain, however many hosts you plug in. A VLAN (virtual LAN) lets you cut one physical switch into several logical switches. Each VLAN is its own broadcast domain. A broadcast sent in VLAN 10 is never sent out of a port that belongs to VLAN 20. BOOK
| Device | Collision domains | Broadcast domains |
| Hub | 1 for all ports | 1 |
| Switch, no VLANs | 1 per port | 1 for the whole switch |
| Switch with VLANs | 1 per port | 1 per VLAN |
| Router | 1 per interface | 1 per interface (broadcasts are not forwarded by default) |

This table is my summary of the book's explanation on pp. 220 to 222 ADDED . The book says the same thing in words: switches break up collision domains, routers break up broadcast domains, and VLANs let a switch do the second job at layer 2.
EXAM CRITICAL
A switch separates collision domains. A VLAN (or a router) separates broadcast domains. Examiners like to swap these two.

Figures 8.3 and 8.4 in plain words. Four hosts are plugged into one switch. With no VLANs (Figure 8.3) all four receive each other's broadcasts. If you configure Host A and Host B as Sales and Host C and Host D as Admin (Figure 8.4), you get two LANs, two subnets and two broadcast domains on the same physical switch, and you did not buy a second switch. The book says all of these mean the same thing: "two LANs, two subnets, two broadcast domains, two VLANs". BOOK
MEMORY TIP

Think of it as a chain: one VLAN = one broadcast domain = (normally) one IP subnet. Strictly, a VLAN is layer 2 and a subnet is layer 3, but the book (p. 240) says to give every VLAN its own subnet. Do that. BOOK
How VLANs make management easier (the book's list, p. 223). BOOK
- Adds, moves and changes are easy: you just put the port in the right VLAN.
- A group that needs more security can sit in its own VLAN, so outsiders cannot talk to it directly.
- VLANs group users by function, not by where they sit.
- VLANs greatly improve security if they are implemented correctly (see 8.1.2 for the warning).
- VLANs increase the number of broadcast domains and make each one smaller.
8.1.1 Broadcast Control

Book p. 223. How many broadcasts a network sees depends on three things: the type of protocol, the applications running, and how those services are used. BOOK Multimedia applications use broadcasts and multicasts a lot. Faulty equipment, poor segmentation and badly designed firewalls make it worse. Common broadcasts you already know are ARP requests and DHCP Discover messages. ADDED

By default a switch filters broadcasts from every port that is not in the same VLAN as the sender. You get the benefits of a switched network without every user sharing one huge broadcast domain. BOOK
WHY THIS MATTERS

Every broadcast interrupts every host in the broadcast domain. Smaller broadcast domains mean less wasted bandwidth and less work for each host's CPU, and a problem in one segment is easier to isolate.
8.1.2 Security

Book pp. 223 to 224. In a flat network the router was supposed to provide security, but that did not work well. Anyone who plugged into the LAN could reach its resources. Anyone could plug a network analyser into a hub and see all traffic. Anyone could join a workgroup just by plugging in. BOOK

With VLANs you control each port and which VLAN it is in. Switches can also be set up to tell a network management station about unauthorised access, and you can place restrictions on the router that routes between VLANs. BOOK
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE
A VLAN is not a security wall on its own. The book says VLANs "greatly enhance network security if implemented correctly". The key words are if implemented correctly. UPDATED

Two classic attacks are switch spoofing (an attacker's PC negotiates a trunk with the switch using DTP) and double tagging (works when the attacker's access VLAN is the same as the trunk's native VLAN). Defences: set every user port to switchport mode access yourself, do not let user ports negotiate, do not use VLAN 1 or the native VLAN for users, shut unused ports, and filter traffic between VLANs with ACLs or a firewall (Chapter 10).
Source status: general networking knowledge plus Cisco Community statements from Cisco staff. The Cisco VLAN security white paper itself was not opened. CHECK
8.1.3 Flexibility and Scalability
Book p. 224. A layer 2 switch only reads the frame, not the network layer, so by default it floods broadcasts. VLANs create smaller broadcast domains at layer 2. BOOK
- A broadcast from a node in one VLAN is not forwarded to ports in a different VLAN. BOOK
- You can add users to a VLAN wherever they are, across one switch or many switches. BOOK
- A broadcast storm from a faulty NIC stays inside the VLAN where it started. It can still hurt that VLAN. BOOK
- When a VLAN gets too big, create more VLANs so fewer users are hit by broadcasts. BOOK
- The book's design tip: keep services local to users where you can, except email and Internet access that everyone needs. BOOK
Quick check 8.1
Q1. A switch has 12 active ports and no VLANs configured. How many broadcast domains does it have?
Answer: B - with no VLANs the whole switch is one broadcast domain. It has 12 collision domains, one per port.
Q2. Name two things that split a network into more than one broadcast domain.
Answer: VLANs on a switch, and routers (each router interface is a separate broadcast domain) - a plain switch does not do it.
Q3. Host A in VLAN 10 sends an ARP request (a broadcast). Which ports receive it?
Answer: Only ports in VLAN 10 (access ports in VLAN 10, plus trunks that carry VLAN 10) - ports in other VLANs never see it.
Q4. True or false: hosts in two different VLANs on the same switch can talk to each other without a router, because they share the same switch.
A. True
B. False
Answer: False - separate VLANs are separate broadcast domains and subnets. You need a layer 3 device to route between them.
Book pages 224 to 229. Tracker rows: 8.2, 8.2.1, 8.2.2. v1.1 objectives 2.1.a, 2.2.a, 2.2.b, 2.2.c. v2.0 objectives 2.1.b, 2.2, 2.2.c.

The idea in plain words. Switch ports are layer 2 interfaces. In this chapter a port is one of two kinds. An access port belongs to one VLAN and talks to ordinary devices. A trunk port carries many VLANs at once and talks to other switches, routers or servers that understand VLAN tags. You choose one or the other for each port, not both. BOOK
|  | Access port | Trunk port |
| Carries | One VLAN (plus an optional voice VLAN) | Many VLANs |
| Frames on the wire | Untagged (no VLAN information) | Tagged with the VLAN ID, except the native VLAN, which is untagged |
| Connects to | PCs, printers, servers, phones, access points | Switch to switch, switch to router, switch to server |
| Does the device know about VLANs? | No. It just thinks it is on a LAN. | Yes. Both ends must understand 802.1Q. |
This table is my summary of pp. 224 to 227 ADDED .
Access ports

- An access port belongs to and carries the traffic of only one VLAN. Traffic is sent and received in its normal form, with no VLAN tag at all. Anything arriving on the port is assumed to belong to the VLAN configured on the port. BOOK
- The VLAN set on the port is called the configured VLAN (or access VLAN) of the port. BOOK
- The attached device does not know which VLAN it is in. The switch removes any VLAN information before it sends a frame out of an access port. BOOK
- Devices on an access link cannot reach devices outside their VLAN unless the packet is routed. BOOK
- In the book's Figure 8.5, two switches are joined by one access link per VLAN (one for Sales, one for Admin). That works, but it uses one port per VLAN on both switches. Trunks fix this. BOOK
Voice access ports

The book (p. 226) says an access port can have a second VLAN for voice traffic, the voice VLAN (it used to be called the auxiliary VLAN). This lets you plug a phone into the switch and a PC into the phone, using one switch port, while keeping the phone and the PC in separate VLANs. It is still an access port. BOOK

How it works (the book does not explain this). The PC's frames pass through the phone untagged and land in the port's data VLAN. The phone tags its own voice frames with the voice VLAN ID. The switch tells the phone which voice VLAN to use, using CDP (Cisco phones) or LLDP-MED (many other phones). ADDED CHECK
| Traffic | Tagged on the wire? | VLAN |
| PC behind the phone (data) | No, untagged | The port's access (data) VLAN, for example VLAN 10 |
| IP phone (voice) | Yes, 802.1Q tag | The voice VLAN, for example VLAN 30 |
EXAM CRITICAL

v2.0 names "Voice over IP phone" (2.2.c) as an edge-host connection you must configure. Know the three lines: switchport mode access, switchport access vlan <data>, switchport voice vlan <voice>. See 8.4.1.
Trunk ports
- The word trunk comes from telephone trunks, which carry many calls at once. A trunk port can carry many VLANs at once. BOOK
- A trunk link is a point-to-point link (100, 1,000, 10,000 Mbps or more) between two switches, a switch and a router, or a switch and a server. BOOK
- By default all VLANs are allowed on a trunk, unless you remove them by hand. BOOK
- If the link between two switches is not a trunk, only the access VLAN of that port crosses it. BOOK
- A trunk to a server can put that server in several VLANs at once, so users do not have to cross a router to reach it. BOOK
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE

VLAN number ranges (clarified). The book says a trunk carries "from 1 to 4,094 VLANs" but "the amount is really only up to 1,001 unless you're going with extended VLANs". That is loosely worded. The real ranges are below. UPDATED
| VLAN IDs | Name | Notes |
| 0 and 4095 | Reserved by 802.1Q | 0 means "priority tag only, no VLAN". 4095 must not be used. |
| 1 | Default VLAN | Every port starts here. It cannot be deleted or renamed. |
| 2 to 1001 | Normal range | Your everyday VLANs. This is the range the book means by "1,001". |
| 1002 to 1005 | Reserved | Old FDDI and Token Ring defaults. Cannot be used, deleted or changed. |
| 1006 to 4094 | Extended range | VTP versions 1 and 2 cannot carry them. On those versions the switch must be in VTP transparent mode to create them. VTP version 3 supports them. |
Status: checked against a Cisco IOS configuration document (official) and Cisco Community posts quoting Cisco documents (secondary). Exact behaviour varies by platform and IOS version CHECK .
8.2.1 Frame Tagging

Book pp. 227 to 228. The idea. When a frame crosses a trunk, the next switch needs to know which VLAN it belongs to. So the sending switch adds a VLAN ID to the frame. That is frame tagging. The book calls a group of switches that share the same VLAN information the switch fabric. Each switch reads the VLAN ID from the tag, looks in its filter (forward) table to decide what to do, and removes the tag when the frame leaves through an access port. BOOK
Worked example (my addition). Host A (VLAN 10) is on SW1 port Fa0/1. Host B (VLAN 10) is on SW2 port Fa0/1. SW1 and SW2 are joined by an 802.1Q trunk. ADDED
| Step | Where | Tag? | What happens |
| 1 | A to SW1 Fa0/1 (access port) | No tag | SW1 assigns the frame to VLAN 10 because of the port's configuration. |
| 2 | Inside SW1 | n/a | SW1 looks up B's MAC address in its VLAN 10 table. The exit port is the trunk. |
| 3 | SW1 to SW2 (trunk) | 802.1Q tag, VLAN 10 | SW1 inserts the tag and recalculates the frame check sequence. |
| 4 | Inside SW2 | n/a | SW2 reads tag 10 and looks up B in its VLAN 10 table. The exit port is an access port. |
| 5 | SW2 Fa0/1 to B (access port) | No tag | SW2 removes the tag. B receives a normal frame. |

Native VLAN and PVID. A trunk port has a default port VLAN ID (PVID). All untagged traffic on that trunk belongs to the PVID VLAN. This VLAN is the native VLAN. It is VLAN 1 by default but can be changed. A frame whose VLAN equals the native VLAN of the outgoing trunk port is sent untagged. All other VLANs are sent tagged. BOOK
EXAM CRITICAL
Native VLAN = the VLAN whose frames cross an 802.1Q trunk untagged. Default is VLAN 1. Both ends of a trunk must use the same native VLAN. This is directly named in v1.1 (2.2.c).
WARNING

Untagged frames arriving on a trunk are put into the native VLAN of that port. The book says in one place that untagged frames go to "the management VLAN" (p. 238). The management VLAN and the native VLAN are separate settings that happen to both be VLAN 1 by default. See 8.4.2. UPDATED
8.2.2 VLAN Identification Methods
Book pp. 228 to 229. There are two ways to tag frames on a trunk: ISL and 802.1Q.

ISL (Inter-Switch Link). Cisco-proprietary. It wraps the whole original frame in a new header and adds a new CRC (frame check). It works at layer 2 and can be used on switch ports, router interfaces and server NICs. The book says Cisco has moved to 802.1Q only. BOOK

IEEE 802.1Q. The open standard. It does not wrap the frame. It inserts a field (the tag) into the existing frame, so the CRC must be recalculated. If you trunk between Cisco and another brand, you must use 802.1Q. BOOK
| Feature | ISL | IEEE 802.1Q |
| Standard | Cisco proprietary | IEEE open standard |
| Method | Encapsulates the frame in a new header and a new CRC | Inserts a 4-byte tag into the frame; CRC recalculated |
| Added size | 30 bytes (26-byte header plus 4-byte CRC) CHECK | 4 bytes |
| Untagged native VLAN | No (every frame is wrapped) CHECK | Yes, one native VLAN per trunk |
| Works with other vendors | No | Yes |
| On current Cisco switches | Not supported on many (for example 2960, 3650, 9200 series) | Supported everywhere |
ISL status: Cisco Community posts quoting a Cisco Press article say the 2960, 3650 and 9200 series support only 802.1Q. This is secondary. UPDATED CHECK
The 802.1Q tag in detail. The tag is 4 bytes and sits between the source MAC address and the original Type/Length field. BOOK The book shows it in Figure 8.7.
| Field | Size | Meaning |
| TPID (Tag Protocol Identifier) | 16 bits | Fixed value 0x8100. It marks the frame as 802.1Q-tagged. Not shown in the book. ADDED |
| PCP (Priority Code Point) | 3 bits | Priority (802.1p, class of service). The book calls it the "user priority field". |
| DEI (Drop Eligible Indicator) | 1 bit | Marks frames that may be dropped first in congestion. The book calls it CFI (Canonical Format Identifier), the old name. UPDATED |
| VID (VLAN Identifier) | 12 bits | The VLAN number. This is the only field you need for the exam. BOOK |
EXAM CRITICAL

The VID is 12 bits, so there are 2^12 = 4,096 values. 0 and 4,095 are reserved, so an 802.1Q frame can identify 4,094 VLANs (1 to 4094). The book gets this right (p. 229). The arithmetic was checked in the Python script.
ADDED (NOT IN THE BOOK)
A tagged frame can be up to 1,522 bytes instead of 1,518, because of the 4-byte tag (IEEE 802.3ac). Status: secondary source. CHECK
WHAT THE BOOK SAYS

The book (p. 229) says the purpose of ISL and 802.1Q tagging is inter-switch VLAN communication, and tags are used only inside the switch fabric and on trunks. They are removed when a frame leaves through an access link.
Quick check 8.2
Q1. Which kind of port removes the VLAN tag before it sends a frame to a PC?
Answer: An access port - the PC does not understand tags.
Q2. Which statement about 802.1Q is true?
A. It is Cisco proprietary.
B. It wraps the frame in a new header and a new CRC.
C. It inserts a 4-byte tag and leaves the native VLAN untagged.
D. It supports only VLANs 1 to 1005.
Answer: C - 802.1Q is the IEEE standard. A is ISL, B describes ISL, and D confuses 802.1Q with the Cisco normal range.
Q3. What is the default native VLAN on a Cisco switch trunk?
Answer: VLAN 1 - it can be changed with switchport trunk native vlan.
Q4. A PC is plugged into an IP phone, and the phone into a switch port with data VLAN 10 and voice VLAN 30. Which frames are tagged?
Answer: The phone's voice frames (VLAN 30). The PC's frames are untagged and go to VLAN 10 - this is why the port still counts as an access port.
Book pages 229 to 231. Tracker row: 8.3. v1.1 objective 2.1.c InterVLAN connectivity. v2.0 objectives 2.1 and 2.1.d.

The idea in plain words. Each VLAN is a separate broadcast domain and a separate subnet. Hosts in the same VLAN talk freely. To send traffic from one VLAN to another you need a layer 3 device that routes between the subnets. BOOK The book shows three ways:
| Method | Links to the switch | Switch port | Host gateway | Good | Bad |

| 1. Router with one interface per VLAN (Fig. 8.8) | One per VLAN | Access, one per VLAN | IP of that router interface | Simple idea | Uses a switch port and a router port for every VLAN. Does not scale. |

| 2. Router on a stick, ROAS (Figs. 8.9, 8.10) | One | Trunk | IP of the router subinterface for that VLAN | One cable. Cheap if you already have a router. | All inter-VLAN traffic crosses one link. Bottleneck and single point of failure. |

| 3. Layer 3 switch with SVIs (Fig. 8.11) | None, it is inside the switch | Access and trunk as normal | IP of the SVI for that VLAN | Fast, built into the switch hardware | Needs a multilayer switch and ip routing. |

Router on a stick. One physical router interface is split into subinterfaces, one per VLAN. Each subinterface gets an encapsulation identifier that says which VLAN's tag it handles, and an IP address in that VLAN's subnet. Each subinterface IP becomes the default gateway of its VLAN. The switch port facing the router is a trunk. The book warns that this creates a bottleneck and a single point of failure. BOOK It is called "on a stick" because a packet from VLAN 10 to VLAN 20 goes up the one cable to the router and comes back down the same cable. ADDED

Layer 3 switch (SVI). Instead of an external router, you create logical interfaces inside a multilayer switch, one per VLAN. They are called switched virtual interfaces (SVIs). The routing happens on the switch backplane, which is faster and more efficient than an external router. BOOK
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE

Exam wording. The book says router on a stick "is what's used on the CCNA objectives for inter-VLAN routing". In v1.1 the objective is 2.1.c "InterVLAN connectivity" (the book's v1.0 text says just "Connectivity"). In the official v2.0 PDF the phrase "router on a stick" does not appear. v2.0 lists switch-to-router connectivity (2.1), 802.1Q trunk interfaces (2.1.b) and the SVI (2.1.d). Learn both ROAS and SVI. UPDATED
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE

Dated hardware advice. On pp. 229 to 231 the book discusses 2600, 2800 and 3560 models, FastEthernet interfaces and the price of used equipment. Ignore the model advice. It is not exam content, and the 2600 and 2800 are end-of-life. What matters is the design idea. UPDATED
Quick check 8.3
Q1. Which inter-VLAN routing method uses subinterfaces?
Answer: Router on a stick - one physical interface is split into one subinterface per VLAN.
Q2. Why is router on a stick a single point of failure and a bottleneck?
Answer: All inter-VLAN traffic goes through one router interface and one cable - if either fails, no VLAN can reach another VLAN.
Q3. In a router-on-a-stick design, what is the default gateway of hosts in VLAN 20?
Answer: The IP address of the router subinterface that handles VLAN 20 - not the physical interface address.
Q4. Which of these needs the ip routing command?
A. A router subinterface
B. A Layer 3 switch with SVIs
C. A Layer 2 switch trunk port
D. An access port
Answer: B - a multilayer switch only routes once ip routing is turned on. Routers route by default.

Book pages 231 to 247. Tracker rows: 8.4, 8.4.1, 8.4.2, 8.4.3. v1.1 objectives 2.1 and 2.2. v2.0 objectives 2.1 and 2.2. The book reuses its Chapter 7 network (switches S1 and S3, a router named ISR). You will build a smaller network of your own in the labs. All outputs marked BOOK are copied in meaning from the book. They were not run by me.
Creating VLANs
Use the global command vlan on a Catalyst switch. This is the book's example on S1, with four VLANs for departments (p. 232). BOOK
Create VLANs 2 to 5 (book p. 232) BOOK
S1(config)# vlan 2
S1(config-vlan)# name Sales
S1(config-vlan)# vlan 3
S1(config-vlan)# name Marketing
S1(config-vlan)# vlan 4
S1(config-vlan)# name Accounting
S1(config-vlan)# vlan 5
S1(config-vlan)# name Voice
S1(config-vlan)# end
- vlan 2 creates VLAN 2 (or opens it if it exists) and enters VLAN configuration mode. Use IDs 2 to 1001 for everyday VLANs.
- name Sales gives it a text label. The name is optional and does not change how frames are forwarded. Without it the name defaults to something like VLAN0002. CHECK
- end (or Ctrl+Z) leaves configuration mode. On classic IOS a VLAN change is applied when you leave VLAN configuration mode. CHECK
- Save your work with copy running-config startup-config.
WHAT THE BOOK SAYS
Extended VLANs (p. 232). The book tries vlan 4000 on a switch in VTP server mode (the default) and gets: "Failed to create VLANs 4000. Extended VLAN(s) not allowed in current VTP mode."
It says extended VLANs (above 1005) are not saved in the VLAN database unless the switch is in VTP transparent mode. BOOK
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE

That is true for VTP versions 1 and 2. VTP version 3 supports the full range 1 to 4094, including in server mode. Status: Cisco IOS document (official) and Cisco Community quoting Cisco documentation (secondary). UPDATED CHECK
Verifying VLANs: show vlan
Output from the book, p. 233 (shortened) BOOK
S1# show vlan
VLAN Name Status Ports
1 default active Fa0/1, Fa0/2, Fa0/3, Fa0/4
Gi0/2
2 Sales active
3 Marketing active
4 Accounting active
5 Voice active
[output cut]
What to notice:
- VLANs 2 to 5 exist but have no ports yet. A VLAN is unused until you assign ports to it. All ports are in VLAN 1 by default. BOOK
- Ports Fa0/15 to Fa0/18 are missing from the list. show vlan shows access ports only, so those four ports must be trunks. Use show interfaces trunk to see trunks. BOOK

On a Layer 3 switch you can turn a physical port into a Layer 3 port with no switchport and give it an IP address, for example a /30 link to a router. v2.0 lists "Layer 2/Layer 3 physical interfaces" (2.1.a). Example: interface gi0/2, no switchport, ip address 10.0.0.1 255.255.255.252 (10.0.0.0/30, usable .1 and .2, calculated). ADDED CHECK

| Command | What you expect |
| show vlan brief | Each VLAN exists and has ports. |
| show interfaces trunk | The router or switch uplink is trunking and allows the VLANs you route. |
| show ip interface brief | Subinterfaces or SVIs are up/up with the right IP. SVI up/down points to autostate (see above). |
| show ip route | A connected route (C) for each VLAN subnet. CHECK |
| ping the gateway, then a host in another VLAN | Ping to the gateway works first. Then the cross-VLAN ping works. |
Quick check 8.4.3
Q1. Write the router commands that make Gi0/0.30 the gateway 192.168.30.1/24 for VLAN 30 (the physical interface is already up).
Answer: interface gi0/0.30, then encapsulation dot1Q 30, then ip address 192.168.30.1 255.255.255.0 - the encapsulation line comes first.
Q2. Does interface fa0/0 on a router create an SVI?
Answer: No. An SVI is created with interface vlan <number> on a Layer 3 switch - the book's wording on p. 245 is wrong.
Q3. An SVI for VLAN 20 shows up/down. Name two possible causes.
Answer: VLAN 20 does not exist or is not active, or no port in VLAN 20 is up (autostate) - also check spanning tree is forwarding on that port.
Q4. Host 192.168.10.77/28: what are the subnet, broadcast and usable range?
Answer: Subnet 192.168.10.64, broadcast 192.168.10.79, usable 192.168.10.65 to 192.168.10.78 - block size 16; 77 falls in the 64 block. Calculated by script.

sections.title: Troubleshooting VLANs, Trunks and Inter-VLAN Routing

content.text: None of this was tested on hardware. Treat the "first check" column as a starting point. CHECK
| Symptom | Likely cause | First check |
| Host cannot reach anything, not even its gateway | Port in the wrong VLAN, or the VLAN does not exist | show vlan brief, show interfaces <int> switchport |

| Hosts in the same VLAN on two switches cannot talk | Link is not a trunk, VLAN not allowed on the trunk, or VLAN missing on one switch | show interfaces trunk on both switches, show vlan brief on both |
| Trunk does not form | Both ends dynamic auto; one end access; encapsulation mismatch | show interfaces <int> switchport on both ends |
| Log: NATIVE_VLAN_MISMATCH | Native VLAN differs between the two ends | Compare the Native vlan column in show interfaces trunk; show spanning-tree inconsistentports |
| One VLAN stopped working after a trunk change | allowed vlan list was replaced and dropped that VLAN | show interfaces trunk; fix with allowed vlan add <id> |
| Works inside the VLAN, not between VLANs | Wrong or missing host gateway; no routing; wrong subinterface or SVI address | Ping the gateway first; show ip interface brief; show ip route |
| ROAS subinterface down | Physical interface shut, or encapsulation dot1Q ID wrong | show ip interface brief; show running-config interface gi0/0.10 |
| ROAS up, one VLAN fails | VLAN not allowed on the switch trunk, or wrong VLAN ID on subinterface | show interfaces trunk on the switch |
| SVI up/down | VLAN missing, or no active port in that VLAN (autostate) | show vlan brief, show ip interface brief |
| Layer 3 switch does not route | ip routing missing | show running-config \| include ip routing |
| Phone gets an address in the data VLAN | Voice VLAN not set, or CDP or LLDP not working | show interfaces <int> switchport, show cdp neighbors |
| Host cannot reach gateway, IP looks fine | Wrong mask or host in a different subnet | Recalculate the subnet and compare host and gateway |
| Topic | Remember |
| VLAN | One VLAN = one broadcast domain = (normally) one subnet. Switches split collision domains, VLANs and routers split broadcast domains. |
| Access port | One VLAN, untagged. Plus optional voice VLAN. Type switchport mode access and switchport access vlan N. |
| Voice VLAN | switchport voice vlan N. Phone tags voice, PC untagged. Switch tells the phone via CDP or LLDP-MED. |
| Trunk | Many VLANs, tagged. All VLANs allowed by default. switchport mode trunk. Add the encapsulation command only on switches that support ISL. |
| 802.1Q tag | 4 bytes: TPID 0x8100, PCP 3 bits, DEI 1 bit (book says CFI), VID 12 bits. 4,094 usable VLANs. |
| ISL | Cisco only, encapsulates, retired. Not on modern switches. |
| Native VLAN | Untagged VLAN on an 802.1Q trunk. Default 1. Must match both ends. Mismatch can block VLANs, not only management. |
| VLAN ranges | Normal 1 to 1005 (1002 to 1005 reserved). Extended 1006 to 4094 (VTP v1/v2 need transparent mode; v3 supports it). |
| DTP | Auto + auto = access. Desirable + auto = trunk. Default is usually dynamic auto. Best practice: static trunk + nonegotiate; static access on user ports. |
| Allowed list | allowed vlan 4,6 replaces the list. Use add, remove, all. |
| Verify | show vlan brief (access ports only), show interfaces trunk, show interfaces <int> switchport. |
| Router on a stick | Trunk to router. Subinterface per VLAN: encapsulation dot1Q N, then ip address. Subinterface IP = host gateway. Bottleneck. |
| SVI / Layer 3 switch | ip routing, then interface vlan N and ip address. SVI is not fa0/0. VLAN must exist and have an active port. |
| New host | Check the port's VLAN first. |

labs.title: VLANs and access ports on one switch

content.text: Goal: create VLANs, assign ports, prove VLANs are isolated. Topology: switch S1 (2960), PC1 on Fa0/1, PC2 on Fa0/2. Set PC1 to 192.168.10.11/24 and PC2 to 192.168.20.11/24, no gateway.
- Create the VLANs (below).
- Assign Fa0/1 to VLAN 10 and Fa0/2 to VLAN 20.
- Verify with show vlan brief.
- Ping PC2 from PC1. Then change PC2 to 192.168.10.13/24 and ping again.
Lab 1 configuration CHECK
S1(config)# vlan 10
S1(config-vlan)# name Sales
S1(config-vlan)# vlan 20
S1(config-vlan)# name Admin
S1(config-vlan)# exit
S1(config)# interface fa0/1
S1(config-if)# switchport mode access
S1(config-if)# switchport access vlan 10
S1(config-if)# interface fa0/2
S1(config-if)# switchport mode access
S1(config-if)# switchport access vlan 20
- Each vlan block creates a VLAN and names it. Each interface block makes the port a static access port in that VLAN.
MEMORY TIP

Expected result. show vlan brief lists Fa0/1 under VLAN 10 and Fa0/2 under VLAN 20. The first ping (different subnets, different VLANs, no router) fails. Why: separate VLANs are separate broadcast domains and there is no layer 3 device. The second ping, with PC2 given an address in the 192.168.10.0/24 subnet, still fails because PC2's port is in VLAN 20, so the ARP broadcast never reaches PC1. This shows that the VLAN, not the IP address, decides who can talk. CHECK
Optional voice step. Add an IP phone in Packet Tracer on a new port, set switchport voice vlan 30, and check show interfaces <int> switchport. Packet Tracer phone behaviour may differ. CHECK

labs.title: Two switches, 802.1Q trunk, allowed VLANs, native VLAN

content.text: Goal: span VLANs across switches, test DTP, break and fix the native VLAN. Topology: S1 and S2 (2960) joined by Gi0/1 on both. PC1 and PC2 on S1 (Fa0/1 VLAN 10, Fa0/2 VLAN 20). PC3 and PC4 on S2 (Fa0/1 VLAN 10, Fa0/2 VLAN 20). Create VLANs 10 and 20 on both switches and assign the ports as in Lab 1.
- Before any trunk config, check the default: show interfaces gi0/1 switchport on both switches. Note the administrative mode. Ping PC3 from PC1.
- Configure the trunk on both switches (below). Ping again.
- Remove VLAN 20 from the trunk with switchport trunk allowed vlan remove 20 on S1 Gi0/1. Test PC2 to PC4.
- Restore with switchport trunk allowed vlan all.
- Change the native VLAN on S1 only to 99. Read the log message. Then make S2 match.
Lab 2 trunk configuration CHECK
S1(config)# interface gi0/1
S1(config-if)# switchport mode trunk
S1(config-if)# switchport nonegotiate
S1(config-if)# switchport trunk native vlan 99
(repeat on S2)
- switchport mode trunk makes the link a permanent trunk. 2960 needs no encapsulation command.
- switchport nonegotiate stops DTP frames. Do the same on both ends.
- switchport trunk native vlan 99 sets the untagged VLAN. You must create VLAN 99 first on both switches (vlan 99).
MEMORY TIP

Expected results. Step 1: the default mode is probably dynamic auto (see 8.4.2), the link is not a trunk, and the ping fails CHECK . Step 2: after the trunk is up, PC1 reaches PC3 and PC2 reaches PC4. show interfaces trunk shows on, 802.1q, trunking. Step 3: PC2 cannot reach PC4 but PC1 still reaches PC3, because only VLAN 20 was removed. Step 5: with S1 native VLAN 99 and S2 still 1, expect a %CDP-4-NATIVE_VLAN_MISMATCH message and possibly spanning-tree PVID inconsistency messages. Check show spanning-tree inconsistentports. After S2 matches, they clear. CHECK Simulator note: Packet Tracer may not show every log message real IOS does.
Extra test (DTP table). Try auto/auto, auto/desirable and trunk/auto on the link and compare with the matrix in 8.4.2. Record each result. CHECK
Goal: route between VLAN 10 and VLAN 20. Topology: Lab 2 plus a router R1 connected to S1 Gi0/2 from R1 Gi0/0. Hosts need gateways: PC1 and PC3 use 192.168.10.1, PC2 and PC4 use 192.168.20.1.
- On S1: interface gi0/2, switchport mode trunk.
- On R1: bring up Gi0/0 and create subinterfaces .10 and .20 (code in 8.4.3).
- Ping the gateway from PC1, then ping PC2 from PC1, then PC4 from PC1.
- Run traceroute (tracert on a PC) from PC1 to PC2.
MEMORY TIP

Expected result. Pings to the gateway work, then PC1 reaches PC2 and PC4. The trace shows 192.168.10.1 (the router) as the first hop. All inter-VLAN traffic goes up and down the one trunk. show ip route on R1 lists C routes for both subnets. If PC1 cannot reach PC2, use the troubleshooting table. CHECK
Goal: replace the router with SVIs. Topology: a multilayer switch MLS1 (3560 in Packet Tracer) with PC1 on Fa0/1 (VLAN 10) and PC2 on Fa0/2 (VLAN 20). Hosts use gateways .1 in their subnet.
Lab 4 configuration CHECK
MLS1(config)# vlan 10
MLS1(config-vlan)# vlan 20
MLS1(config-vlan)# exit
MLS1(config)# interface fa0/1
MLS1(config-if)# switchport mode access
MLS1(config-if)# switchport access vlan 10
MLS1(config-if)# interface fa0/2
MLS1(config-if)# switchport mode access
MLS1(config-if)# switchport access vlan 20
MLS1(config-if)# exit
MLS1(config)# ip routing
MLS1(config)# interface vlan 10
MLS1(config-if)# ip address 192.168.10.1 255.255.255.0
MLS1(config-if)# no shutdown
MLS1(config-if)# interface vlan 20
MLS1(config-if)# ip address 192.168.20.1 255.255.255.0
MLS1(config-if)# no shutdown
- ip routing turns on routing. Each interface vlan creates the SVI that acts as the gateway. The two VLANs exist and each has an active port, so the SVIs can come up.
MEMORY TIP

Expected result. show ip interface brief shows Vlan10 and Vlan20 up/up. PC1 pings PC2. Now remove PC2's port from VLAN 20 (shut Fa0/2) and watch Vlan20 go down (autostate), then bring it back. Then delete ip routing (no ip routing) and see the cross-VLAN ping fail. CHECK

quizzes.title: VLANs and Inter-VLAN Routing — review questions

questions.source: Q1. A switch has 12 active ports and no VLANs configured. How many broadcast domains does it have?
questions.q: A switch has 12 active ports and no VLANs configured. How many broadcast domains does it have?
questions.why: with no VLANs the whole switch is one broadcast domain. It has 12 collision domains, one per port.

questions.source: Q2. Name two things that split a network into more than one broadcast domain.
questions.q: Name two things that split a network into more than one broadcast domain.
questions.why: VLANs on a switch, and routers (each router interface is a separate broadcast domain) - a plain switch does not do it.

questions.source: Q3. Host A in VLAN 10 sends an ARP request (a broadcast). Which ports receive it?
questions.q: Host A in VLAN 10 sends an ARP request (a broadcast). Which ports receive it?
questions.why: Only ports in VLAN 10 (access ports in VLAN 10, plus trunks that carry VLAN 10) - ports in other VLANs never see it.

questions.source: Q4. True or false: hosts in two different VLANs on the same switch can talk to each other without a router, because they share the same switch.
questions.q: True or false: hosts in two different VLANs on the same switch can talk to each other without a router, because they share the same switch.
questions.why: False - separate VLANs are separate broadcast domains and subnets. You need a layer 3 device to route between them.

questions.source: Q1. Which kind of port removes the VLAN tag before it sends a frame to a PC?
questions.q: Which kind of port removes the VLAN tag before it sends a frame to a PC?
questions.why: n access port - the PC does not understand tags.

questions.source: Q2. Which statement about 802.1Q is true?
questions.q: Which statement about 802.1Q is true?
options: It wraps the frame in a new header and a new CRC.
It inserts a 4-byte tag and leaves the native VLAN untagged.
questions.why: 802.1Q is the IEEE standard. A is ISL, B describes ISL, and D confuses 802.1Q with the Cisco normal range.

questions.source: Q3. What is the default native VLAN on a Cisco switch trunk?
questions.q: What is the default native VLAN on a Cisco switch trunk?
questions.why: VLAN 1 - it can be changed with switchport trunk native vlan.

questions.source: Q4. A PC is plugged into an IP phone, and the phone into a switch port with data VLAN 10 and voice VLAN 30. Which frames are tagged?
questions.q: A PC is plugged into an IP phone, and the phone into a switch port with data VLAN 10 and voice VLAN 30. Which frames are tagged?
questions.why: The phone's voice frames (VLAN 30). The PC's frames are untagged and go to VLAN 10 - this is why the port still counts as an access port.

questions.source: Q1. Which inter-VLAN routing method uses subinterfaces?
questions.q: Which inter-VLAN routing method uses subinterfaces?
questions.why: Router on a stick - one physical interface is split into one subinterface per VLAN.

questions.source: Q2. Why is router on a stick a single point of failure and a bottleneck?
questions.q: Why is router on a stick a single point of failure and a bottleneck?
questions.why: ll inter-VLAN traffic goes through one router interface and one cable - if either fails, no VLAN can reach another VLAN.

questions.source: Q3. In a router-on-a-stick design, what is the default gateway of hosts in VLAN 20?
questions.q: In a router-on-a-stick design, what is the default gateway of hosts in VLAN 20?
questions.why: The IP address of the router subinterface that handles VLAN 20 - not the physical interface address.

questions.source: Q4. Which of these needs the ip routing command?
questions.q: Which of these needs the ip routing command?
questions.why: a multilayer switch only routes once ip routing is turned on. Routers route by default.

questions.source: Q1. Write the commands to make Fa0/5 a static access port in VLAN 20.
questions.q: Write the commands to make Fa0/5 a static access port in VLAN 20.
questions.why: interface fa0/5, then switchport mode access, then switchport access vlan 20 - the VLAN must also exist (vlan 20), or be created for you on some platforms.

questions.source: Q2. You create VLAN 20 with vlan 20 and name Sales. Which hosts are in it now?
questions.q: You create VLAN 20 with vlan 20 and name Sales. Which hosts are in it now?
questions.why: None. A VLAN is unused until you assign ports to it - all ports stay in VLAN 1 until configured.

questions.source: Q3. Why are trunk ports not listed in show vlan?
questions.q: Why are trunk ports not listed in show vlan?
questions.why: show vlan lists access ports only - use show interfaces trunk to see trunks.

questions.why: switchport voice vlan 30 - the port stays an access port; the phone tags its own frames with VLAN 30.

content.text: Q1 A switch has 12 active ports and no VLANs configured. How many broadcast domains does it have?
Answer: B - with no VLANs the whole switch is one broadcast domain. It has 12 collision domains, one per port.
Q2 Name two things that split a network into more than one broadcast domain.
Answer: VLANs on a switch, and routers (each router interface is a separate broadcast domain) - a plain switch does not do it.
Q3 Host A in VLAN 10 sends an ARP request (a broadcast). Which ports receive it?
Answer: Only ports in VLAN 10 (access ports in VLAN 10, plus trunks that carry VLAN 10) - ports in other VLANs never see it.
Q4 True or false: hosts in two different VLANs on the same switch can talk to each other without a router, because they share the same switch.
A. True
B. False
Answer: False - separate VLANs are separate broadcast domains and subnets. You need a layer 3 device to route between them.
Q1 Which kind of port removes the VLAN tag before it sends a frame to a PC?
Answer: A - n access port - the PC does not understand tags.
Q2 Which statement about 802.1Q is true?
A. It is Cisco proprietary.
B. It wraps the frame in a new header and a new CRC.
C. It inserts a 4-byte tag and leaves the native VLAN untagged.
D. It supports only VLANs 1 to 1005.
Answer: C - 802.1Q is the IEEE standard. A is ISL, B describes ISL, and D confuses 802.1Q with the Cisco normal range.
Q3 What is the default native VLAN on a Cisco switch trunk?
Answer: VLAN 1 - it can be changed with switchport trunk native vlan.
Q4 A PC is plugged into an IP phone, and the phone into a switch port with data VLAN 10 and voice VLAN 30. Which frames are tagged?
Answer: The phone's voice frames (VLAN 30). The PC's frames are untagged and go to VLAN 10 - this is why the port still counts as an access port.
Q1 Which inter-VLAN routing method uses subinterfaces?
Answer: Router on a stick - one physical interface is split into one subinterface per VLAN.
Q2 Why is router on a stick a single point of failure and a bottleneck?
Answer: A - ll inter-VLAN traffic goes through one router interface and one cable - if either fails, no VLAN can reach another VLAN.
Q3 In a router-on-a-stick design, what is the default gateway of hosts in VLAN 20?
Answer: The IP address of the router subinterface that handles VLAN 20 - not the physical interface address.
Q4 Which of these needs the ip routing command?
A. A router subinterface
B. A Layer 3 switch with SVIs
C. A Layer 2 switch trunk port
D. An access port
Answer: B - a multilayer switch only routes once ip routing is turned on. Routers route by default.
Q1 Write the commands to make Fa0/5 a static access port in VLAN 20.
Answer: interface fa0/5, then switchport mode access, then switchport access vlan 20 - the VLAN must also exist (vlan 20), or be created for you on some platforms.
Q2 You create VLAN 20 with vlan 20 and name Sales. Which hosts are in it now?
Answer: None. A VLAN is unused until you assign ports to it - all ports stay in VLAN 1 until configured.
Q3 Why are trunk ports not listed in show vlan?
Answer: show vlan lists access ports only - use show interfaces trunk to see trunks.
Q4 Which command adds VLAN 30 as a voice VLAN on an access port?
Answer: switchport voice vlan 30 - the port stays an access port; the phone tags its own frames with VLAN 30.
Q1 Both ends of a link are dynamic auto. What is the result?
Answer: A - n access port (no trunk) - neither end sends the first DTP request.
Q2 A trunk allows VLANs 10, 20 and 30. You type switchport trunk allowed vlan 30. What does it allow now?
Answer: Only VLAN 30 - the plain form replaces the list. Use add to add.
Q3 Which log message tells you the native VLANs differ between two Cisco switches?
Answer: %CDP-4-NATIVE_VLAN_MISMATCH - spanning tree may also log PVID inconsistency messages.
Q4 switchport trunk encapsulation dot1q is not accepted on a 2960. Why? When do you need it?
Answer: The 2960 supports only 802.1Q, so the command does not exist. You need it on switches that support both ISL and 802.1Q, such as the 3560 - check the platform before you type it.
Q1 Write the router commands that make Gi0/0.30 the gateway 192.168.30.1/24 for VLAN 30 (the physical interface is already up).
Answer: interface gi0/0.30, then encapsulation dot1Q 30, then ip address 192.168.30.1 255.255.255.0 - the encapsulation line comes first.
Q2 Does interface fa0/0 on a router create an SVI?
Answer: No. An SVI is created with interface vlan <number> on a Layer 3 switch - the book's wording on p. 245 is wrong.
Q3 An SVI for VLAN 20 shows up/down. Name two possible causes.
Answer: VLAN 20 does not exist or is not active, or no port in VLAN 20 is up (autostate) - also check spanning tree is forwarding on that port.
Q4 Host 192.168.10.77/28: what are the subnet, broadcast and usable range?
Answer: Subnet 192.168.10.64, broadcast 192.168.10.79, usable 192.168.10.65 to 192.168.10.78 - block size 16; 77 falls in the 64 block. Calculated by script.
Q1 A switch has 12 access ports in use, spread over 3 VLANs. How many collision domains and broadcast domains does it have?
Answer: 12 collision domains and 3 broadcast domains - one collision domain per port, one broadcast domain per VLAN.
Q2 Which port type sends and receives frames without a VLAN tag?
A. Trunk port (all frames)
B. Access port
C. Routed port only
D. None
Answer: B - an access port sends untagged frames.
Q3 How many bytes does an 802.1Q tag add to a frame?
Answer: B - 4 bytes. 26 and 30 relate to ISL.
Q4 How many VLANs can the 802.1Q VLAN ID identify, and why?
Answer: 4,094 (1 to 4094) - 12 bits gives 4,096 values; 0 and 4,095 are reserved.
Q5 Which VLAN IDs are the normal range on Cisco switches, and which are reserved within it?
Answer: 1 to 1005, where 1002 to 1005 are reserved (and VLAN 1 is the default) - extended range is 1006 to 4094.
Q6 Which VLAN carries untagged frames on an 802.1Q trunk by default?
A. VLAN 0
B. VLAN 1
C. VLAN 99
D. The voice VLAN
Answer: B - the native VLAN, VLAN 1 by default.
Q7 A PC and a phone share one switch port. Which command gives the phone VLAN 30?
Answer: switchport voice vlan 30 - the PC stays in the access VLAN.
Q8 Switch A has native VLAN 99 and switch B has native VLAN 1 on the same trunk. What can you see?
Answer: A - %CDP-4-NATIVE_VLAN_MISMATCH log message, and possibly spanning-tree PVID inconsistency that blocks VLANs on the port - it is not only a management issue.
Q9 Which command shows allowed, active and forwarding VLANs on trunks?
A. show vlan brief
B. show interfaces trunk
C. show ip route
D. show running-config vlan
Answer: B - show vlan brief does not list trunk ports.
Q10 A trunk allows VLANs 10, 20 and 30. You enter switchport trunk allowed vlan 20. What is allowed now?
Answer: Only VLAN 20 - the plain form replaces the list. Use add.
Q11 Two ports are both dynamic auto. Do they trunk?
A. Yes
B. No, they stay access
Answer: B - auto waits for the other end to ask.
Q12 One end is dynamic desirable and the other dynamic auto. Result?
Answer: A - trunk - desirable actively asks, and auto accepts.
Q13 One end is switchport mode trunk with switchport nonegotiate; the other is dynamic auto. What happens?
Answer: The auto end never becomes a trunk, because no DTP frames arrive. The link is mismatched and does not work properly - set both ends to trunk.
Q14 What must be turned on before SVIs route between VLANs on a Layer 3 switch?
A. no switchport
B. ip routing
C. ip default-gateway
D. vtp mode transparent
Answer: B - ip routing.
Q15 In encapsulation dot1Q 20, what does 20 mean?
Answer: The VLAN ID whose tagged frames this subinterface handles - it is not the subinterface number.
Q16 In router on a stick, what is the default gateway of hosts in VLAN 30?
Answer: The IP address of the router subinterface for VLAN 30 -
Q17 Why is router on a stick a bottleneck and a single point of failure?
Answer: A - ll inter-VLAN traffic uses one router interface and one link - a Layer 3 switch avoids this.
Q18 Hosts in VLAN 10 can ping the router subinterface, but VLAN 30 cannot. The trunk on the switch allows 10 and 20 only. Fix?
Answer: switchport trunk allowed vlan add 30 - do not retype the plain form or you may drop others.
Q19 An SVI shows up/down. Give three conditions that must hold for it to come up.
Answer: The VLAN exists and is active; at least one layer 2 port in that VLAN is up; that port is in spanning-tree forwarding - this is SVI autostate.
Q20 Host 172.16.5.200/26. Give the subnet, broadcast and usable range.
Answer: Subnet 172.16.5.192, broadcast 172.16.5.255, usable 172.16.5.193 to 172.16.5.254 - calculated by script.
Q21 What is the smallest mask for a VLAN with 45 hosts, and for one with 120 hosts?
Answer: /26 (62 usable) and /25 (126 usable) - calculated by script.
Q22 Host 10.1.40.77/27. What is the subnet and broadcast address?
Answer: Subnet 10.1.40.64, broadcast 10.1.40.95, usable .65 to .94 - calculated by script.

Q24 When do you need switchport trunk encapsulation dot1q?
Answer: Only on switches that support both ISL and 802.1Q, such as a 3560 - a 2960 does not have the command.
Q25 True or false: putting hosts in different VLANs makes a network secure by itself.
A. True
B. False
Answer: B - VLAN hopping attacks exist. Set ports to access explicitly, do not use VLAN 1 or native for users, and filter between VLANs.
